— five findings from the research

01
August Problem

Students returning in August receive a harder exam than they sat in June

Schema burden averages 45.4 in August vs. 37.6 in June sittings. Students below 55 average 35.1% in August vs. 10.7% in June. These are students completing a graduation requirement — and the instrument meets them with greater demand.

02
Skill Gap

The exam rewards source extraction far more reliably than historical context and causation

Across 5 USH sittings, the gap between binary CR item success and extended CRQ performance averages 24.9 percentage points. Reading what a document says is not the same skill as knowing why it was written — and the exam scores them differently.

03
Centering

US History centers dominant racial and national frames more often than Global II

USH items more often center white, national, elite, and state-sanctioned institutional perspectives. Global II distributes attention more broadly across class, labor, coloniality, gender, religion, and race. The two exams students take are not measuring the same version of "historical thinking."

04
Transition

The GHG→USH transition has an 8.3-point standard deviation — the exams measure different things

Among 93 students in the primary cohort transition, mean scores rose +1.8 points — but with 8.3-point SD. Seven students dropped more than 10 points. The same preparation that succeeds in Global II does not reliably transfer to US History's demands.

05
Hidden Pattern

Resistant voices score higher on neutrality challenge — and are perceived as less neutral

In the Re:Source library, dominant and institutional sources score 2.43–2.75 on the neutrality challenge scale. Resistant and community voices score 4.34. The sources that name power are read as biased. The sources that exercise it are read as neutral.

06
Root Cause

The exam doesn't just disadvantage students by being hard — it rewards the wrong answer

Distractor analysis suggests that thorough formation in the dominant cultural gaze — what the curriculum trains students to do — leads reliably to wrong answers on the most demanding items. This is not a design flaw. It is a structural feature.

💡 Why This Matters

The theory of change behind Questioning Neutrality.

Assessments are not neutral.

Every assessment reflects choices: which questions are asked, whose voices count as evidence, what kinds of thinking are rewarded. When we treat assessments as objective, we make those choices invisible — and invisible choices tend to reproduce existing inequities.

The "implied student" problem.

Every assessment imagines a student. It assumes background knowledge, cultural familiarity, language comfort, and prior experience. When that implied student doesn't match the actual students in front of us, the assessment measures cultural proximity rather than historical thinking.

Perspective is a historical skill, not a political opinion.

Including marginalized voices in assessments isn't about ideology — it's about rigor. The College Board's Historical Thinking Skills require students to consider perspective, context, and bias. A source set drawn entirely from dominant perspectives cannot generate the intellectual friction necessary for genuine historical analysis.

The Triangulation Framework.

Strong source sets include voices that stand in productive tension with each other: a government order alongside the letter of someone affected by it; a corporate regulation alongside a worker's petition. This tool operationalizes that principle by scoring your source sets on perspective diversity, gaze, and interpretive richness.

This is not about making assessments easier.

Equity and rigor are not in tension. This tool helps you design assessments that are harder in the right ways — that require genuine historical thinking, not cultural familiarity. The goal is assessments where every student can demonstrate what they actually know.

📐 Scoring Guide & Rubric

How this tool evaluates assessments, and how to export a Google Apps Script for spreadsheet integration.

Equity Scoring Dimensions

DimensionWhat it MeasuresScore Range
Perspective GazeWhose experience does this source center? (1=outsider looking in, 5=insider speaking for themselves)1–5
Neutrality ChallengeHow much does this source challenge the assumption of a "neutral" view?1–5
Interpretive RichnessHow many different valid interpretations does this source support?1–5
Access LoadHow much cultural/linguistic background knowledge does this source assume? (1=high assumption, 5=low assumption)1–5
Rigor SupportHow well does this source support AP/Regents-level historical thinking skills?1–5

Perspective Categories

CategoryDefinitionExamples
DominantVoice of those with institutional or social powerGovernment orders, court rulings, colonial records
ResistantVoice challenging or outside dominant power structuresWorker petitions, enslaved narratives, anti-imperial speeches
InstitutionalOfficial institutional voice (can be progressive or conservative)Constitutions, treaties, congressional debates
AmbiguousPerspective that cuts across simple dominant/resistant categoriesInsider critiques, complex negotiations, dual-audience texts

Part I

Is this a consistent exam sitting to sitting?

Both exams fail this standard not because students change, but because the instrument does.

Viz 1
Pass rates, below-55 rates, and schema burden across all 12 sittings
August and January retake sittings shown in orange. Schema burden (dashed, right axis) measures the spread between easiest and hardest item on each sitting.
35.1%
avg below-55, August
10.7%
avg below-55, June
45.4
schema burden avg, Aug
37.6
schema burden avg, June
Pass 65+Below 55Dashed = schema burden

Data

Aug sittings avg 35.1% below-55 vs 10.7% for June. GHG Aug 2025: 11.1% pass, 63% below 55. Schema burden tracks with failure.

For Mott Haven students

19 students who sat GHG both June and August dropped from 55.3 to 47.7. The instrument changed; the students did not.

What should change

System: Mandate schema burden comparability. School: Report Aug/June as separate cohorts. Teacher: Name the harder instrument explicitly.

Viz 2
Score distributions by sitting -- IQR and median with 65-pt pass threshold
June IQRAug/Jan IQR
Viz 3
Item success rate stability across sittings (red = high SD, amber = moderate, green = stable)
USH item stability
GHG item stability
Viz 4
CivLit 34A vs 34B -- 66-point swing across GHG sittings

Data

34B ranges 14.7% to 85.7% -- a 66-pt swing. 34A avg 47.3%, 34B avg 25.6%. An item with 66-pt variance is not measuring a stable competency.

For Mott Haven students

Students cannot prepare for something the exam itself does not reliably define. For Black and Brown students, democratic vocabulary is not neutral -- it carries the history of exclusion.

What should change

System: Equate CivLit items before release. School: Do not treat CivLit performance as reflecting stable civic knowledge. Teacher: Teach democratic vocabulary as a language with a history.

Viz 5
Near-miss students: % within 10 pts of passing, and avg pts from 65

Data

USH Aug 2024: 89% of failing students within 10 pts of passing. Across sittings, near-miss students avg 4.3-7.0 pts from passing. They extract at 52-61% but contextualize at 29-36%.

For Mott Haven students

These students are not failing because they cannot think historically. They are 5-7 points from graduating. The gap has a name: historical contextualization. That skill is teachable.

What should change

System: Fund targeted near-miss intervention. School: Track near-miss rate as a key equity metric. Teacher: Contextualization using Re:Source high-DIF source sets is the direct intervention.

Part II

Do Mott Haven students have an equitable experience relative to the state?

Equity requires comparable outcomes AND comparable access to the knowledge the exam assumes.

Viz 6
School vs Bronx district vs state pass rates, and neutrality challenge by voice type
Pass rate comparison (June sittings)
Neutrality challenge by voice type (Re:Source, n=781)

Data

School June avg: USH 69.9%, GHG 69.7%. State: USH 76%, GHG 73%. Bronx district: USH 58%, GHG 61%. The gap between this school and the state is approximately 15-18 pts.

For Mott Haven students

This gap is not an ability gap -- it is the quantified distance between the implied reader of the exam and the actual reader. State averages are pulled by districts whose students more closely match the exam assumptions.

What should change

System: Disaggregate state pass rates by school demographic context. School: Use Re:Source as counter-archive in curriculum planning. Teacher: Name the equity gap explicitly.

Viz 7
DIF gap by source voice type and near-miss vs passing rate by source type
Avg DIF gap by source voice type (pts)
Near-miss vs passing rate by source type
Viz 8
Source characteristics: era and speaker identity vs near-miss performance
Near-miss correct rate by era of source
Near-miss vs passing rate by speaker identity
Viz 9
Schema demand vs success -- the equity gradient (USH 31.9-pt spread, GHG 19.4-pt spread)
USH schema demand gradient
GHG schema demand gradient

Data

USH: LOW items succeed at 63.1%, VERY HIGH at 31.2% -- a 31.9-point spread. GHG gradient is shallower (19.4 pts), confirming GHG rewards argument over canonical recall more than USH does.

For Mott Haven students

High-schema items are items where students rich in community historical knowledge do not activate the specific canonical frame the exam rewards. The 31-pt spread is not ability vs no ability -- it is whose prior knowledge matches.

What should change

System: Schema demand should be a documented item specification. School: Curriculum must name what canonical knowledge each unit builds. Teacher: Re:Source schema burden coding makes this visible before you select a source.

Viz 10
Extraction vs historical context -- USH (24.9-pt gap) and GHG (7.3-pt gap)
USH: extraction vs context by score band
GHG: extraction vs context by score band

Data

USH near-miss: extract at 57%, contextualize at 31% -- 26-pt gap. GHG shows 7.3-pt gap -- because GHG rewards argumentation over canonical recall.

For Mott Haven students

These students have the reading skill. What they lack is the specific American historical canon USH extended items presuppose. Students who thrive in GHG by reading closely now meet an exam that demands prior canonical knowledge.

What should change

System: CRQ items should make required contextual knowledge explicit. School: GHG-to-USH sequence must include explicit periodization instruction. Teacher: Re:Source source sets around high-DIF CRQ topics are the direct intervention.

Viz 11
Open response vs binary CR equity ratios -- near-miss students perform better on essays
Binary CR equityEssay equity
Viz 12
Historical thinking skill success rates -- USH has a 27.5-pt gap, GHG only 7.4 pts
USH skill family success rates
GHG skill family success rates
Viz 13
DIF severity -- average and maximum gaps by exam sitting

Data

GHG Jun 2025: 42.9% of items flagged. GHG Aug 2024 max gap: 80 pts -- near-miss 10%, passing 90% on the same item. 6 SEVERE DIF items identified across all sittings.

For Mott Haven students

DIF measures which students have the cultural schema the item presupposes. A near-miss student who fails CivLit34B is not failing because they cannot reason civically -- the item assumes a specific democratic vocabulary that was never named as curriculum.

What should change

System: Publish DIF statistics for all released items. School: Use DIF patterns in instructional data review. Teacher: Use high-DIF items as entry points for explicit schema building.

Part III

Distractor analysis: what kind of knowing does each wrong answer represent?

When near-miss and passing students select different answers, they are demonstrating different epistemological positions.

Viz 14
Near-miss vs passing choice distributions -- most epistemically significant items
Left = near-miss (55-64), right = passing (65-84). Highlighted slice = dominant choice. Entropy shown below each donut.

Data

43 item-sitting pairs show near-miss and passing students selecting different dominant answers. Near-miss entropy avg 1.47 vs passing 1.27. Near-miss students are more certain -- and more wrong. Their certainty is curriculum formation.

For Mott Haven students

QuantCrit frames this as measurement that encodes dominant epistemologies as correct. The wrong answer is not cognitive error -- it is evidence of a different but valid historical frame that the exam key does not recognize as authoritative.

What should change

System: Release distractor distribution data by school demographic context. School: Post-exam analysis should examine which answer was selected, not just which items were missed. Teacher: Teach what makes the exam answer correct AND why the student answer is historically defensible.

Viz 15
Epistemic framework comparison -- what interpretive tradition does the near-miss dominant choice reflect?
Part IV

Item Response Theory analysis

IRT reveals not just which items discriminate but what they discriminate on -- historical thinking or cultural schema access.

Viz 16
IRT: discrimination vs difficulty -- the essay is the best psychometric item on both exams
Essay/Ext CRQBinary CRCivic Lit

Data

USH Essay (a=1.47, rpbi=0.65) and GHG P3 (a=1.11, rpbi=0.55) are the highest-discrimination items on both exams. USH CR33 has a=0.25 -- near-zero, providing almost no information about historical thinking ability.

For Mott Haven students

Items doing the most sorting work on graduation are often the least valid measures of historical thinking. CR33 near-zero discrimination means it is measuring schema access, not skill. Students who pass it are not more capable -- they are more culturally proximate to what it assumes.

What should change

System: Remove items with a under 0.4 and rpbi under 0.2. School: IRT grading should be part of annual data review. Teacher: Essay instruction has the best instructional return of any item type on either exam.

Viz 17
Item Characteristic Curves -- steep ICC = high discrimination, flat = culturally loaded
USH Essay (a=1.47, Excellent)

Viz 18
Test Information Function -- both exams peak below the pass threshold
USH TIF (peaks theta=-1.0)GHG TIF (peaks theta=-0.6)Pass threshold ≈ theta=0

Data

USH TIF peaks at theta=-1.0; GHG at theta=-0.6. The pass threshold sits at approximately theta=0. Both exams are significantly more informative below passing than above it. They are gatekeeping instruments, not learning measurement instruments.

For Mott Haven students

The exam is sharpest exactly where these students are. Every DIF-flagged item, every schema-loaded question, every distractor divergence -- these happen with maximum measurement consequence for students at theta -0.5 to 0. These students are not on the margins of the exam. They are at its center.

What should change

System: Publish TIF distributions. An exam whose information peaks at failure should not be a graduation requirement without equity review. School: Near-miss band support is the highest-leverage school-level intervention. Teacher: Your students are where the exam is most precise.

Part V

Teaching critical consciousness and graduation access simultaneously

The data points toward a third path: teach the canon as a tool, not a truth.

Viz 21
Near-miss intervention: the contextualization gap, USH and GHG
USH: extraction vs context gap
GHG: extraction vs context gap

The third path

Teach the canon as a tool, not a truth. Name it as one interpretive tradition among many, practice it for the exam, then teach the counter-narrative alongside it through Re:Source. Students who can hold both frames are better positioned to identify which one the exam is asking for and deploy it strategically without their critical consciousness being colonized by it.

The distractor is a curriculum audit. When 70% of near-miss students converge on the same wrong answer with high confidence, that is not confusion -- it is evidence that the curriculum formed them toward one frame. The pedagogical move: make the exam frame visible as a choice.

Graduation is the floor. Critical consciousness is the ceiling. These are not in conflict. The essay ICC proves it: the most psychometrically valid item on both exams is also the most equitable. It rewards argument -- and argument is the same skill that builds critical consciousness.
